alt: A grid of surveys and interviews (postal and telephone, online, self-completion, structured, unstructured and group) with a strength and a limitation of each, and types of survey question.
caption: More structure brings reliability; less structure brings depth.

alt: A grid of observation types, laboratory and field experiments, longitudinal studies and qualitative and quantitative secondary sources, each with a strength and a limitation, plus classic examples.
caption: Natural settings gain validity; controlled settings gain cause and effect.

alt: A chain from population to sampling frame to sample, then six types of sample: random, systematic and stratified random; quota, multistage and snowball.
caption: The sample can only be as good as the frame it is drawn from.

alt: Religiosity can be operationalised as worship, prayer or belief, each giving a different result. Two variables that move together may both be caused by a third factor. Notes list interviewer bias, the Hawthorne effect and social desirability.
caption: How you measure, and what else might explain a link, shape every finding.

alt: The TREND routine for quantitative data: title and units, read extremes, examine change and comparison, note percentage points versus relative change, and doubt the source. A note gives the routine for qualitative extracts.
caption: TREND turns an unseen table into marks.

alt: A bar chart of fictional data: urban households using mobile money rose from 30% in 2015 to 74% in 2025, rural from 12% to 51%. The gap widened in percentage points while rural use grew faster in relative terms.
caption: Percentage points and relative change can tell different stories.
